title: The problem Docker solves
idea: Docker tackles the "it works on my machine" problem. It ships the app together with its environment, so every machine runs the same setup.
points: Your app's environment is the Node.js version, packages and system libraries around its code.
Machines set up by hand drift apart: a laptop, a test server, production.
Two apps on one server can need different Node.js versions.
A new teammate installs Docker and runs the image, not a setup checklist.

hero.title: Setup by hand or by image

left.title: Install on every machine
items: Each machine installs Node.js and packages itself
Versions drift between laptop, test and production
A bug appears on one machine and not another
New teammates follow a setup checklist

right.title: Ship the environment
items: The image holds Node.js, packages and your code
Every machine runs the same image
Two apps can use different Node.js versions
New teammates install Docker, then run the image

hero.verdict: One image replaces many hand-built setups.

pitfalls: Do not expect Docker to fix bugs; it only keeps the environment consistent.
Settings and secrets still differ per environment; keep them out of the image.

quiz.q: The API crashes only on a teammate's laptop. How does an image help?
options: It rewrites your code for each machine
Both machines run the same Node.js and packages
It fixes bugs in your JavaScript
It copies your laptop's files to theirs
quiz.why: The image carries Node.js, packages and code together, so both machines run one environment. A genuine bug in your code still crashes.

takeaway: When behavior differs by machine, compare the environments too.

starters: Why does the same code behave differently on two machines?
What goes inside an image and what stays outside?
Do I still need Node.js installed on my laptop?
